deep.reconstruction:
This page is a later fair copy, headed 'Abschrift 1879 Nov 21; original in the hands of Dr. Meyerstein'. It reproduces Gauss's short report 'Resultate der Prüfung eines von Hrn Meierstein angefertigten Maasstabes'. The report comes from his work on the Hannoverian standard measures (Normalmaaße, both length and capacity) in the later 1830s and 1840s.

Setting: a scale made by the instrument maker M. Meyerstein carries 640 divisions, each very nearly 1 mm. Their absolute size did not matter for the purpose. What mattered was how uniform the divisions were.

Definitions (modern notation, mine): let x_k be the actual position of division line k, for k = 0..640, and L = x_640 - x_0 the total length. The tabulated 'Fehler' is
  f(k) = [x_k - x_0 - k*L/640] / u,
where u is the micrometer-screw unit, with 438.6 screw parts per 'millimetre' (strictly, per L/640). Hence f(0) = f(640) = 0 by construction, which matches the table.

Method: Gauss states only that the comparator and the procedure would be described elsewhere. He notes that the procedure does not accumulate errors and gives all results nearly equal reliability. This suggests the intervals were compared against a fixed reference length or adjusted jointly, rather than read off by chaining successive intervals. That interpretation is mine; no computation appears on the page.

Table content: 66 tested lines, including the endpoints. The lines are concentrated at multiples of 4, 8, 16 and 32, plus a few clusters of adjacent lines (31/32, 226/227, 264/265, 351/352, 420/421, 508–512, 608/609).

Pattern: almost all errors are negative. The largest is -15.46 at line 420 and -15.22 at line 448. In physical terms this is 15.46/438.6 mm, about 0.035 mm, or 35 µm. The errors show a broad trough around lines 80–130 and 340–480, and return toward 0 near 550–640. The only positive value is +0.73 at line 560.

There is no derivation on the page; it is a report of measurement results.
errors: No mathematical errors can be assessed; the page reports measured data only.
Spelling is inconsistent: 'Meierstein' in the title, 'Meyerstein' in the header. The person is Moritz Meyerstein, Göttingen instrument maker.
The entry at line 536 is written '-1,6(0)' with a hesitant or bracketed last digit. Its value is uncertain in the copy.

results.what: Calibration table of the division errors of a 640-part (≈mm) scale relative to uniform division of its total length. Errors are given in micrometer-screw parts (438.6 per division).
results.modern_name: Calibration of a line scale / division-error determination with a comparator
results.usually_credited_to: Standard 19th-century metrology (Bessel, Gauss, later Thiesen and others for scale-calibration schemes)

results.what: Claim of a calibration procedure in which errors do not accumulate and all lines are determined with nearly equal precision. The method is not described on this page.
results.modern_name: Non-cumulative scale calibration (e.g. comparison of all intervals with a standard interval, or least-squares adjustment of interval comparisons)
results.usually_credited_to: Bessel / Gauss in the 1830s; later systematised by Hansen and Thiesen

deep.surprise_reason: This is an experimental metrology report from Gauss's well-documented work with Meyerstein on the Hannoverian standard measures. Gauss's involvement there is well known (cf. Werke XI). The page has no new mathematics, only a data table and a remark about an unpublished non-cumulative method.

checkable.asserts: One micrometer-screw part = 1/438.6 mm ≈ 0.00228 mm (2.28 µm).
The largest error (-15.46 parts, line 420) corresponds to about 0.0352 mm ≈ 35 µm.
The error at line 448 (-15.22 parts) is about 0.0347 mm.
The only positive error (+0.73, line 560) is about 0.0017 mm.
With f(k)=x_k - k L/640, the endpoints have zero error by definition, consistent with f(0)=f(640)=0 in the table.

transcription_corrections: Line 536: the image shows '-1,6(0)' with a circled or uncertain final digit; the reading '-1,60[?]' is appropriate.
Line 244 (second column) could also be read as 247 in the image. 244 fits the multiples-of-4 pattern (240, 244, 248) and is likely correct.
Otherwise the machine transcription agrees with the image.
